title: Freezing and Melting
summary: How heat and cold change water between ice and liquid, why ice expands and floats, and how other materials melt at their own temperatures.
poll: Water is the most interesting material on Earth.

versions.title: Ice and Water
versions.text:
Put a cup of water in the freezer. Wait a few hours. Now look. The water is hard. It is ice!

Water is a liquid. It can flow. It can spill. Ice is a solid. It keeps its shape.

Cold makes water freeze. Water turns to ice at zero degrees. That is very cold.

Heat makes ice melt. Hold an ice cube in your hand. Your hand is warm. The ice gets wet. It turns back to water. Then it can freeze once more.

Ice takes up more room than water. Fill a glass jar to the top. Put it in the freezer. The jar may crack!

Ice is light, too. It floats in your drink.

Some things melt fast. Chocolate melts in a warm hand. Iron does not. It needs a huge fire.

Snow can fall in the north of Saudi Arabia. It falls in some winters. Then the sun comes out. The snow melts.

versions.title: Ice and Water
versions.text:
Fill a cup with water. Put it in the freezer. Wait a few hours. Then look at it. The water is hard now. It has turned to ice!

Water is a liquid. A liquid can flow and spill. It takes the shape of its cup. Ice is a solid. A solid keeps its own shape.

When water gets very cold, it starts to freeze. Water turns to ice at zero degrees.

Heat makes ice melt. Hold an ice cube in your warm hand. Soon your hand gets wet. The ice turns back into water. You can freeze it and melt it again and again.

Here is a strange fact. Ice takes up more space than water. Fill a glass jar to the top and freeze it. The jar may crack!

Ice is also lighter than water. That is why ice cubes float in your drink.

Things melt at different heats. Chocolate melts in a warm hand. Iron melts only in a very hot fire.

In some winters, snow falls in the north of Saudi Arabia. When the sun warms it, the snow melts.

versions.title: Freezing and Melting
versions.text:
Put a cup of water in the freezer. Wait a few hours. When you open the door, the water is hard and cold. It has turned into ice!

Water can be a liquid or a solid. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its cup. A solid, like ice, keeps its own shape.

When water gets cold enough, it starts to freeze. Water freezes at zero degrees. When ice gets warm, it starts to melt. Ice melts at the same mark. That mark is zero degrees.

Heat makes the change. Hold an ice cube in your hand. Heat from your warm skin goes into the ice. It melts into water. Put the water back in the freezer, and it will freeze again.

Water does something odd when it freezes. It takes up more space! A glass bottle full of water can crack in a freezer. Ice is also lighter than the same amount of water. So ice cubes float.

Each thing melts at its own heat. Chocolate melts in a warm hand. Iron melts only in a very hot fire.

In winter, snow sometimes falls on the mountains in the north of Saudi Arabia. When the sun warms the ground, the snow melts.

versions.title: Freezing and Melting
versions.text:
On a hot summer day, a cold drink full of ice cubes feels great. Have you ever watched the ice cubes slowly shrink? They are changing from one form to another.

Water can be a liquid or a solid. A liquid flows and takes the shape of whatever holds it. A solid, such as ice, keeps its own shape.

When water loses enough heat, it starts to freeze. Pure water freezes at zero degrees Celsius. When ice gains heat, it starts to melt, and this also happens at zero degrees. So freezing and melting are opposite changes at the same mark.

You can test this yourself. Hold an ice cube in your palm. Heat moves from your warm hand into the ice, and it melts into a small puddle. Put that water back in the freezer, and it will freeze into ice again.

Water has a strange habit. Most things shrink when they freeze, but water grows bigger. A full glass bottle of water can crack in a freezer. Because ice takes up more space, it is lighter than the same amount of water, so it floats.

Each thing melts at its own heat. Chocolate melts in a warm hand. But iron needs a fire hotter than 1,500 degrees.

In some winters, snow covers the mountains near Tabuk in the north of Saudi Arabia. When the sun comes back, the snow melts. The water soaks into the ground.

versions.title: Freezing and Melting
versions.text:
On a hot summer afternoon, a glass of cold juice full of ice cubes feels wonderful. But if you leave the glass on the table, the ice cubes slowly shrink and vanish. Where do they go? They do not disappear at all. They simply change from a solid into a liquid.

Everything around us is made of tiny particles that are far too small to see. In a solid, such as ice, the particles are packed tightly together. They shake in place but cannot move around, so a solid keeps its shape. In a liquid, such as water, the particles can slide past each other. That is why a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.

When ice gains heat, its particles shake faster and faster. At zero degrees Celsius, they break free from their places, and the ice begins to melt. When water loses heat, the opposite happens. Its particles slow down and lock into place, and the water begins to freeze. Pure water freezes and melts at the same temperature.

Scientists call these changes reversible, because they can go backward. You can freeze water into ice, melt it, and freeze it again many times.

Water also acts in a strange way. Most materials shrink when they freeze, but water does the opposite. Its particles line up in a pattern with extra space, so ice expands. A full glass bottle of water can crack in a freezer. Because ice takes up more space, it is lighter than the same amount of water, and it can float. This helps living things in cold countries. Ice forms on top of a lake, and fish stay alive in the water below.

Each material melts at its own temperature. Chocolate melts in a warm hand, while iron needs a furnace hotter than 1,500 degrees.

In some winters, snow covers the mountains near Tabuk in northern Saudi Arabia. When the sun returns, the snow melts and soaks into the ground.

Water also behaves in an unusual way. Most materials shrink when they freeze, but water does the opposite. Its particles line up in a pattern with extra space between them, so ice expands. Each material melts at its own temperature. Chocolate melts in a warm hand, while iron needs a furnace hotter than 1,500 degrees.

In some winters, snow covers the mountains near Tabuk in northern Saudi Arabia. When the sun returns, the snow melts and the water soaks into the ground.

versions.text:

They have not actually disappeared; they have changed from a solid into a liquid, which is one of the most common changes in nature.

In a liquid, such as water, the particles are able to slide past one another, so a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.

When ice gains heat, its particles vibrate faster and faster. At zero degrees Celsius, they break free from their fixed positions, and the ice begins to melt. When water loses heat, the opposite occurs: its particles slow down and lock into place, and the water begins to freeze. Pure water freezes and melts at exactly the same temperature.

Scientists describe these changes as reversible, because they can be undone. Water can be frozen into ice, melted, and then frozen again as many times as you like.

This property helps living things in cold countries, where ice forms a layer on top of a lake while fish survive in the water underneath.

Every material melts at its own temperature. Chocolate melts in a warm hand, whereas iron requires a furnace hotter than 1,500 degrees.

In some winters, snow covers the mountains near Tabuk in northern Saudi Arabia. When the sun returns, the snow melts and the water soaks into the ground.

versions.title: Freezing and Melting: The Science of Changing States
versions.text:
On a scorching summer afternoon, a glass of cold juice packed with ice cubes is wonderfully refreshing. Yet if the glass is left on a table, the ice cubes gradually shrink and vanish. They have not really disappeared; they have changed from a solid into a liquid, which is one of the most familiar transformations in nature.

All matter is made of molecules, particles far too small to see even with an ordinary microscope. In a solid such as ice, water molecules are held tightly in a regular pattern called a crystal, and although they vibrate, they cannot leave their positions. In liquid water, the molecules still attract one another, but they can slide past each other, which is why water flows and takes the shape of its container.

When ice absorbs heat, its molecules vibrate faster until, at zero degrees Celsius, they break out of the crystal and the ice begins to melt. This temperature is called the melting point of ice. When water loses heat, the reverse occurs: the molecules slow down, lock into the crystal pattern, and the water freezes at the same temperature. Something surprising happens during melting: while ice is melting, its temperature stays at zero degrees, because the heat it absorbs is used to break the crystal apart instead of warming it. Freezing works the opposite way and releases heat, and because both changes can be undone, scientists call them reversible.

Water also behaves differently from most materials: the majority of substances shrink when they freeze, but the crystal pattern of ice contains open spaces, so water expands by about nine percent. A sealed glass bottle full of water may therefore crack in a freezer. Since the same amount of ice occupies more space, it is less dense than liquid water, which explains why ice floats. This unusual property protects living things: in cold countries, ice forms a layer on top of a lake, while fish continue to swim in the liquid water below.

Every substance has its own melting point. Chocolate melts at a temperature slightly below that of the human body, so it softens in a warm hand, whereas iron does not melt until it reaches roughly 1,500 degrees.

These changes are not limited to laboratories, for in some winters, snow settles on the mountains near Tabuk in northern Saudi Arabia, and when the sun returns, the snow melts and soaks into the ground.

versions.title: Freezing and Melting: The Science of Changing States
versions.text:
On a scorching summer afternoon, a glass of chilled juice packed with ice cubes is wonderfully refreshing, yet if the glass is abandoned on a table, the ice cubes gradually shrink and vanish. They have not genuinely disappeared; they have changed from a solid into a liquid, which is one of the most familiar transformations in the natural world.

All matter is composed of molecules, particles far too small to observe even with an ordinary microscope. In liquid water, the molecules still attract one another, but they can slide past each other, which explains why water flows and adopts the shape of its container.

When ice absorbs heat, its molecules vibrate more energetically until, at zero degrees Celsius, they break out of the crystal and the ice begins to melt; this temperature is known as the melting point of ice. When water loses heat, the reverse occurs: the molecules slow down, lock into the crystal pattern, and the water freezes at the identical temperature. Something remarkable happens during melting. While ice is melting, its temperature remains at zero degrees, because the heat it absorbs is used to dismantle the crystal rather than to warm it, and freezing works the opposite way by releasing heat. Because both changes can be undone, scientists classify them as reversible.

Water also behaves differently from most materials. The majority of substances contract when they freeze, but the crystal pattern of ice contains open spaces, so water expands by approximately nine percent. A sealed glass bottle full of water may consequently crack in a freezer. Since the same quantity of ice occupies more space, it is less dense than liquid water, which explains why ice floats. This unusual property protects living organisms: in cold countries, ice forms an insulating layer on top of a lake, while fish continue to swim in the liquid water beneath it.

Every substance possesses its own melting point. Chocolate melts at a temperature slightly below that of the human body, so it softens in a warm hand, whereas iron does not melt until it reaches roughly 1,500 degrees.

These transformations are not limited to laboratories. In certain winters, snow settles on the mountains near Tabuk in northern Saudi Arabia, and when the sun returns, the snow melts and soaks into the ground.

questions.stem: According to the article, at roughly what temperature does iron melt?
options: 1,500 degrees
100 degrees
37 degrees
Zero degrees
questions.why: The article says iron does not melt until it reaches roughly 1,500 degrees.

wrong.B: That is far too low for iron.
wrong.C: That is near body temperature, where chocolate softens.
wrong.D: Zero degrees is the melting point of ice.

questions.stem: In the article, ice is described as less dense than liquid water. What does dense mean here?
options: How cold a material feels
How fast molecules move
How much matter is packed into a space
How shiny and bright a crystal looks in the light
questions.why: Ice takes up more space for the same amount of water, so it has less matter packed into each space.

wrong.A: Density is not about how cold something feels.
wrong.B: Speed of molecules is about heat, not density.
wrong.D: Density has nothing to do with shine.

questions.stem: A glass of ice water stays near zero degrees until the ice is gone. What best explains this?
options: The glass blocks all heat from entering.
The heat being absorbed is used to break the ice crystals apart.
Water cannot ever be warmer than zero degrees.
The ice releases heat into the water.
questions.why: The article explains that melting ice stays at zero degrees because absorbed heat is used to break the crystal apart instead of warming it.

wrong.A: Heat does enter; that is what melts the ice.
wrong.C: Water can be much warmer; the article mentions warm hands and furnaces.
wrong.D: Freezing releases heat; melting absorbs it.

questions.stem: Chocolate stays firm in a cool room but melts in your mouth. What can you infer?
options: Chocolate has no melting point.
Your mouth is colder than the room.
Chocolate is denser than iron.
Its melting point is between room temperature and body temperature.
questions.why: The article says chocolate melts slightly below body temperature, so a cooler room keeps it solid while a warm mouth melts it.

wrong.A: The article says every substance has its own melting point.
wrong.B: A mouth is warmer than a cool room.
wrong.C: The article does not compare their density.

questions.stem: How does the freezing point of water compare with its melting point?
options: They are the same temperature.
Freezing happens at a higher temperature.
Melting happens at a much lower temperature.
They change every winter.
questions.why: The article says water freezes at the same temperature at which ice melts: zero degrees Celsius.

wrong.D: The article does not say these temperatures change.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe ice forming on top of a lake?
options: To warn readers not to swim in winter
To compare frozen lakes with the warm seas near Saudi Arabia
To show how water's unusual behavior helps living things
To explain why fish eat ice
questions.why: The lake example shows that because ice floats, fish can survive in the liquid water beneath it.

wrong.A: The article gives no swimming warning.
wrong.B: The sea is not compared with lakes.
wrong.D: The article never says fish eat ice.
